title: Exploring the MicroRNA Landscape in Cardiac Amyloidosis: Molecular Insights and Clinical Applications
abstract: BACKGROUND: Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is an increasingly recognized cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, resulting from myocardial deposition of misfolded amyloid fibrils derived predominantly from transthyretin (ATTR wild-type [ATTRwt] or variant [ATTRv]) or immunoglobulin light chains (AL). Despite advances in noninvasive imaging and disease-modifying therapies, delayed diagnosis remains common, and clinically actionable molecular biomarkers for early detection, phenotypic discrimination, and therapeutic monitoring are limited. MicroRNAs (miRNAs), small noncoding regulators of post-transcriptional gene expression, have emerged as key modulators of cardiovascular remodeling and systemic amyloid biology. METHODS: We performed a comprehensive review of experimental, translational, and clinical studies to evaluate the role of miRNAs in transthyretin and light-chain cardiac amyloidosis, incorporating data from myocardial tissue analyses, circulating miRNA profiling, and mechanistic studies in cellular and animal models. RESULTS: Dysregulated miRNA networks contribute to amyloid-induced cardiac injury by modulating mitochondrial energetics, oxidative stress, inflammation, fibrosis, proteostasis, and neurocardiac signaling. Specific miRNAs, including members of the miR-21, miR-29, and miR-30 families, as well as miR-150-5p and miR-339, have been associated with amyloid burden, adverse myocardial remodeling, plasma cell biology, and disease severity. Distinct circulating and tissue miRNA signatures differentiate transthyretin from light-chain cardiac amyloidosis and correlate with functional status, heart failure biomarkers, and clinical outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: MiRNAs represent promising diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers in cardiac amyloidosis and offer mechanistic insights into disease pathogenesis. Integration of miRNA profiling with multimodality imaging and emerging RNA-based therapeutics may enable earlier diagnosis and support precision management of amyloid-related heart failure.

title: Abstract 4368251: Mitochondrial-Targeted Therapies in Ischemic Cardiomyopathy: A Systematic Review of Preclinical and Clinical Evidence (2000–2025)
abstract: Background: Ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM) is characterized by energy failure, oxidative stress, and cardiomyocyte death—processes heavily influenced by mitochondrial dysfunction. This systematic review evaluates mitochondrial-targeted therapies in ICM across preclinical and clinical studies published between 2000 and 2025. Methods: We searched PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science for studies targeting mitochondrial pathways in ICM models. Eligible studies included pharmacologic agents, peptides, gene therapies, and mitochondrial transplantation in in vitro, animal, or human settings. Key outcomes—ejection fraction, infarct size, fibrosis, and mitochondrial function—were extracted and summarized. Results: A total of 112 studies (67 animal, 25 in vitro, 20 clinical) met inclusion. Mitochondria-targeted antioxidants such as MitoQ and Elamipretide (SS-31) consistently reduced infarct size and improved mitochondrial function in rodent models; SS-31 also showed hemodynamic benefit in canine heart failure but only modest improvement in human trials. mPTP inhibitors (e.g., cyclosporine A) reduced infarcts in small animal studies but failed in large clinical trials. Fission inhibitors (e.g., Mdivi-1, P110) preserved mitochondrial morphology and enhanced survival post-infarction. Gene therapies enhancing mitochondrial proteins (e.g., Bcl-2, SIRT3, PGC-1α) improved cardiac energetics and function in animals. Mitochondrial transplantation showed promise in restoring myocardial bioenergetics in preclinical studies and early human cases. Discussion: Mitochondrial-targeted therapies address key ICM mechanisms—oxidative damage, permeability transition, disrupted dynamics, and impaired biogenesis. While preclinical results are strong, translation to humans remains limited. Challenges include timing of delivery, tissue targeting, and variability in human mitochondrial health. Combination therapies and personalized approaches may enhance efficacy. Conclusion: Mitochondrial therapies show high potential in modifying ICM pathophysiology. Further clinical trials, precision targeting, and combination strategies are needed to translate preclinical successes into durable patient outcomes.

title: Abstract 4362767: Combination therapy with phosphodiesterase 5 and neprilysin inhibitors synergistically offsets the development of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
abstract: Background: Cyclic GMP (cGMP) preserves cardiac structure and function, and impaired cGMP signaling contributes to the pathogenesis of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). cGMP levels are regulated by synthetic pathways triggered by NO or natriuretic peptides (NP) and degradatory mechanisms involving phosphodiesterases (PDEs; hydrolyse cGMP) and neprilysin (inactivate NP). Indeed, the expression/activity of PDEs and neprilysin are increased in pre-clinical models and patients with HFrEF. Aim: To evaluate the therapeutic potential of dual inhibition of PDE5 and neprilysin in preventing the pathogenesis of HFrEF. Methods: Wild type (WT), NO (GC-1α -/- ) and NP (GC-A -/- ) -sensitive guanylyl cyclase null mice underwent abdominal aortic constriction (AAC; increased afterload) or sham and received the PDE5 inhibitor sildenafil (Sild; 30mg/kg/day; p.o.) and/or the neprilysin inhibitor racecadotril (Race; 30mg/kg/day; p.o.). Changes in heart morphology/function were assessed via echocardiography. Hearts were sectioned and stained to determine cardiomyocyte size and fibrosis. Underlying molecular changes were investigated by qPCR. Results: AAC induced cardiac dysfunction characterised by decreased ejection fraction (EF%: sham 65.8±3.9, AAC 53.6±5.2), increased left ventricle/body weight ratio (LV/BW: sham 3.26±0.07, AAC 4.37±0.08), and greater cardiac fibrosis (%: sham 0.9±0.09, AAC 5.2±1.04; all n=14-15; *P<0.05). In combination, sildenafil and racecadotril promoted cGMP signalling and ameliorated AAC-induced cardiac dysfunction, reversing compromised contractility (EF%: Sild 46.3±0.9, Race 54.5±0.8, Sild+Race 60.6±1.2), left ventricular hypertrophy (LV/BW: Sild 4.5±0.1, Race 3.9±0.2, Sild+Race 3.9±0.1), and cardiac fibrosis (%: Sild 1.6±0.2, Race 5.9±2.6, Sild+Race 1.5±0.5); dual therapy was broadly more effective than either drug alone (all n=15; *P<0.05 versus one or both monotherapies). AAC elevated mRNA expression of markers of cardiac dysfunction, hypertrophy and fibrosis (e.g. BNP, Col3/4A, MMP2) which were significantly reduced by combination treatment. The positive pharmacodynamic profile of dual therapy was maintained in GC-1α -/- mice but absent in GC-A -/- animals implying efficacy was underpinned by augmentation of NP bioactivity (rather than NO). Conclusions: Concomitant blockade of PDE5 and NEP offers a novel approach for the treatment of HFrEF driven by synergistic augmentation of NP signaling. title: Inflammatory cytokines and immune signalling in heart failure: mechanisms, models, and emerging therapies
abstract: Inflammation plays a central role in the pathophysiology of heart failure (HF), and contributes to disease progression, morbidity and mortality. However, the relationships between inflammatory cytokines and different HF subtypes are complex, heterogeneous and bidirectional. In this review, we examine inflammatory pathways, biomarker profiles and comorbidities in HF with reduced, mildly reduced and preserved ejection fraction, and summarize evidence on the use of high-sensitivity C-reactive protein as a biomarker for systemic inflammation in HF. We provide insights into emerging methodologies for biomarker discovery in HF, and discuss the use of animal models to elucidate underlying mechanisms and test potential treatment strategies. Finally, we provide an overview of the therapeutic landscape, touching on past challenges and future opportunities for the development of targeted anti-inflammatory therapies in HF.

title: Diastolic dysfunction persists 3 months after surgical revascularization in a large animal model of hibernating myocardium
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Diastolic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction secondary to coronary artery disease is associated with a significant morbidity and mortality. Diastolic dysfunction due to chronic myocardial ischemia is an important clinical entity though recovery of diastolic relaxation with revascularization is poorly understood. A swine model of hibernating myocardium (HM) was used to assess systolic and diastolic myocardial recovery following coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). METHODS: Study animals included 18 juvenile pigs who underwent placement of a constrictor around the left anterior descending artery to gradually create chronic ischemia without infarction. Study groups included 5 healthy age- and weight-matched controls, 6 HM animals without revascularization, 7 HM + CABG + 1 month recovery and 5 HM + CABG + 3 months recovery. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was used to assess global systolic and diastolic function at rest and with dobutamine stress. Histopathology assessed tissue structural and molecular changes. RESULTS: Systolic and diastolic myocardial function were significantly depressed in HM. Both improved with CABG; however, diastolic relaxation remained significantly impaired even at 3 months post-CABG compared with controls. Histological analysis showed interstitial fibrosis in HM tissue with residual fibrosis seen post-CABG. Alpha-smooth muscle actin stain identified myofibroblasts in both HM and post-CABG animals. CONCLUSIONS: In a large animal model of HM, diastolic dysfunction persists under stress despite CABG and is present even after 3 months of recovery. Persistent fibrosis and diastolic stiffness prevent full recovery. These findings highlight a therapeutic need for pharmacologic or regenerative adjunctive therapies at the time of revascularization.

title: The border zone after myocardial infarction: clarification of terminology and proposal for a new definition
abstract: The border zone (BZ) resulting from a myocardial infarction (MI) has been a subject of scientific interest for decades, but the concept is now used to describe different phenomena without a clear consensus about the meaning. While historically the term referred to a region existing during the acute phase of MI, in recent decades it has predominantly been used to describe the area immediately adjacent to infarcted tissue in the chronic phase. As a result, identical terms are being used to describe phenomena that, while overlapping from a pathophysiological perspective, are not identical. Adopting a standardized definition that can be used to operationalize the term in pre-clinical and clinical research is needed to integrate findings from different methodologies. Based on a historical overview of BZ concepts and identification of knowledge gaps, we suggest a conceptual working definition that can be employed across different research fields. In the 1970s, articles that used the term BZ were concerned with the acute phase of MI, i.e. hours to days after the insult.1 The BZ was described as a region that was exposed to ischaemia (i.e. oxygen levels low enough to limit mitochondrial function), but that did not develop into infarcted tissue. It therefore surrounded an ‘infarct core’ (Figure 1A). In current terminology, the full region exposed to ischaemia is called the ‘area-at-risk’, the infarct core is sometimes referred to as ‘condemned myocardium’, and surrounding tissue ‘salvageable myocardium’.2 The aim of acute treatment is to keep the infarcted area as small as possible compared to the area at risk, i.e. to maintain a high ‘myocardial salvage index’ (Figure 1B). (A) The border zone (BZ) is a region of viable myocardial tissue adjacent to the infarct. (B) In the acute phase, the area-at-risk (AAR) comprises two zones that are dynamic in time. When the situation has stabilized, the fraction of salvable-to-affected myocardium is the so-called ‘myocardial salvage index’ (MSI). (C) Between the infarct (1) and the distal tissue (3), there is a BZ of viable but abnormal tissue (2). The BZ consists of two populations of cells, which are defined by their history of ischaemia. The arrows indicate that the infarct may increase even in the chronic stage and that cells in the distal myocardium may become affected by direct effects from the infarct and become a part of the BZ. During the historical development of MI research, the concept of a BZ sparked controversy. Some claimed that such a region did not exist at all, and that the transition from infarct to surrounding myocardium was abrupt. Part of this was due to differences between animal models used in research, e.g. dogs were commonly used in early studies. Compared to other species, dogs have a notably high level of collateralized perfusion, and therefore develop infarcts with a distinctly graded exposure to ischaemia.3 The complex situation of these early studies has clinical relevance since, like post-MI dogs, MI patients with chronic coronary syndrome develop significant collateralization. However, even without significant collateralization, patients and animals can develop patchy infarcts after ischaemia and reperfusion, due to a spectrum of tolerance to ischaemia amongst myocardial cells. The historical definition of BZ does not capture these nuances. In the last few decades, the term BZ has mostly been used in studies of much later stages after MI, when a stable region of scar tissue has developed. In this literature, the BZ denotes a conceptual region of tissue surrounding the infarcted area. However, several definitions have been used to operationalize the term in research. These can be grouped into anatomical and functional definitions. Anatomical definitions comprise distance-based approaches, which employ thresholds for wall thickness or microstructural tissue composition.4,5 Indirectly, MR studies using thresholds for contrast enhancement, and histological studies, which compare staining with different properties, also fall into this category. Functional definitions of the BZ comprise descriptions of abnormal contractility despite preserved perfusion, altered electrophysiology, or spatial differences in gene expression.6–8 Despite differences in the definitions used, the accumulated knowledge that has resulted from studies of the BZ is considerable. We know that the region surrounding infarcted tissue has cells with altered gene expression and ultrastructure; that the tissue exhibits altered cellular composition and organization; and that innervation and vascularization are abnormal.9 However, the different definitions used to gain these insights have likely contributed to reduced reproducibility and prevented convergence of data from different technologies. Examples of remaining knowledge gaps include pinpointing the causes and extent of altered electrophysiology for BZ cardiomyocytes, their foundation in altered gene expression, and the drivers for continued remodelling even after the scar is established. As a starting point for further research, we suggest a unifying definition of the BZ: The BZ is a region of viable myocardium immediately adjacent to the infarcted area, with functional properties that are distinct from distal tissue. Infarcted tissue (zone 1): The scar. At some point after the onset of ischaemia, this zone would be defined as the ‘condemned myocardium’. The BZ (zone 2), comprised of: ○ Post-ischaemic tissue with abnormal properties (2a): This zone comprises cells that experienced ischaemia, but survived. This could be due to collateral blood supply, oxygen diffusion, reperfusion, or a combination of these. This zone corresponds to the classical term ‘salvaged myocardium’. During the initial ischaemic insult, zone 2a and 1 together define the AAR. ○ Tissue that never experienced ischaemia but which is still affected by the infarct (2b): This zone comprises cells exhibiting properties distinct from the distal myocardium due to proximity to the scar. This cell population is small in the acute and early chronic phase but exhibits a dynamic expansion over time due to influence from its neighbouring regions (zone 1 and 2a). Distal myocardium (zone 3): Tissue that has not suffered any (direct) effect from the infarct, i.e. comprising cells that have (i) not experienced reduced coronary circulation and (ii) are sufficiently distal to the infarct to not suffer the marked effects seen in the BZ. It is important to note that the endocardium and epicardium may curtail the zones described above, so that in the transmural direction, only zones 1, 2a, and/or 2b may be observed. An example of a such a ‘peninsula infarct’ structure is the well-studied epicardial BZ that develops in the dog post-MI, where a modified myocardial rim, in terms of both structural and electrophysiological properties, persists over the surface of a scar.10 Our BZ definition is fundamental and conceptual, and therefore distinct from most of today’s more operational definitions. The proposed approach is also flexible, as it allows the user to choose which properties of the myocardium that are considered relevant. Furthermore, the conceptual definition is able to encompass the highly complex pathology resulting from ischaemia and reperfusion injury, and can therefore be easily adopted for research models aligned with modern MI treatment practises. Although this flexibility will inevitably introduce a source of variability in the BZ definition, it also places demand on the user to be accurate in their description of their methods, and to support their selection of defining myocardial properties. Our unifying and adaptable definition of the BZ is intended to advance research on the BZ towards an integrated understanding, which reconciles decades of insights from a wide range of technologies and leads to targeted interventions. Espe, PhD, is a Senior researcher at the Institute for Experimental Medical Research at Oslo University Hospital/University of Oslo and an Associate professor at the University of Oslo. He holds a Master’s degree in physics and a PhD in medical imaging from the University of Oslo. Dr. Espe’s research is dedicated to advancing medical imaging, with a particular focus on assessment of the cardiac function-structure relationship utilizing cardiovascular magnetic resonance. He works at the crossroads of medicine and physics. Espe’s research focuses on developing and utilizing novel imaging techniques to deepen our understanding of cardiac mechanics, particularly in relation to heart disease. His aim is not just to better understand the complexities of cardiac pathophysiology; he is also working to enhance diagnostic strategies in cardiovascular medicine while gaining new insights into how the heart fundamentally operates. William E. Louch, originally from Nova Scotia, Canada, received his PhD in Pharmacology from Dalhousie University. Following post-doctoral positions at the University of Leuven, Belgium and the University of Oslo, Norway, Louch became Professor of Medicine at the University of Oslo in 2015, and Secretary General of the International Union of Physiological Sciences in 2025. Louch’s research group links whole-heart function to the structure and function of cardiomyocytes, with particular focus on functional units called dyads that trigger calcium release and cellular contraction. His group has shown that dyads exhibit impressive plasticity, supporting both compensatory remodelling in health but decompensation and arrhythmia during disease and ageing. Critically, Louch’s work has identified distinct cellular mechanisms underlying heart failure with reduced and preserved ejection fraction. This insight has helped explain the utility of existing heart failure treatments, but also led to the ongoing testing of novel therapies targeting these mechanisms. The ultimate goal of this work is to relieve the burden of cardiac disease with treatments tailored to the individual patient. Godfrey L. Smith is Professor of Cardiovascular Physiology at the University of Glasgow’s School of Cardiovascular and Metabolic Health. His research focuses on cardiac electrophysiology and excitation-contraction coupling, and includes the use of advanced biophysical techniques including widefield optical mapping and multiphoton confocal microscopy. He uses a number of animal models but the majority of his animal work uses rabbit models of cardiac pathology. Recent papers include cellular mechanisms for arrhythmic behaviour associated with LQT and with a cardiac scars. In 2012, he co-founded Clyde Biosciences Ltd., a University of Glasgow spin-out, where he serves as Chief Scientific Officer and Director. The company specializes in cardiac safety pharmacology, based primarily on human stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes to assess drug-induced cardiotoxicity. This work has led to a number of research projects using human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes including regenerative medicine approaches to cardiac repair and novel assay systems to test cardiotoxicology of chemotherapy agents. Godfrey is a member of the Academia Europaea (2023-) and has held senior offices in scientific societies including president of the European Society of Cardiology Working Group in Cardiac Cellular Electrophysiology (2012–2000) and the Health and Environmental Sciences Institute (USA). He holds an honorary chair at Imperial College London (2012-), at the National University for Science and Technology, Trondheim, (2006–2021), and in 2023 was appointed as a visiting researcher at the Institute of Experimental Medical Research at the University of Oslo). Mathis Korseberg Stokke is a Full Professor of Translational Cardiology and Head of the Institute for Experimental Medical Research at Oslo University Hospital and the University of Oslo. His research group covers the full spectrum of translational research on arrhythmias and electrophysiology ranging from cellular studies and animal models to clinical research. The group's research mainly focuses on mechanisms underlying ventricular arrhythmias after myocardial infarction, calcium-dependent arrhythmias, and arrhythmias associated with CPVT, HCM, and pre-mature ventricular complexes. He maintains clinical work as a Consultant Cardiologist in the Arrhythmia Unit at Oslo University Hospital, with a particular focus on patients with pre-mature ventricular complexes. He has a Master's degree in Health Administration, and is on several boards and committees at Oslo University Hospital. He has initiated and led regional and national networks for cardiovascular researchers and students in Norway.

title: Passive Predetermination of the Heart: A Cross-Domain Evidence Synthesis from Embryogenesis, Birth Transition, and Allometric Scaling
abstract: Cardiac physiology has accumulated a set of core observational facts—including the necessity of pulsation, sinoatrial node autonomous pacing, all-or-none action potential, topological differentiation of arteries and veins, the near-absence of cardiomyocyte division, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, tachycardia-induced heart failure, age-dependent decline in maximum heart rate, and the irreversible progression of atrial fibrillation—that are currently dispersed across separate domains of electrophysiology, hemodynamics, and pathophysiology. This paper proposes that these facts can be coherently organized within a single physical framework: the heart is the dissipation center geometrically predetermined at the moment of energy injection in a multicellular aggregate. Three independent categories of publicly available data are synthesized to evaluate this proposal: (1) cross-species embryogenesis timelines in 16 vertebrate species, (2) clinical data of birth circulatory transition in humans and animal models, and (3) cross-species allometric scaling relationships. The embryogenesis data show that the timing of the first heartbeat converges on a narrow somite-stage range across species with gestation lengths differing by an order of magnitude, consistent with a diffusion-limit trigger, although the critical variable—embryo cross-sectional thickness at first heartbeat—has not been systematically measured in any species, representing an open empirical gap. The birth transition data reveal a strict temporal sequence in which physical pressure and oxygen partial-pressure changes precede and drive functional closure of the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus, with no documented instances of reversed causality. The allometric scaling data, analyzed using phylogenetic generalized least squares regression across 214 mammalian species, demonstrate that body mass alone explains 94.7% of the variance in heart rate (Pagel's lambda = 0.89), while ecological variables contribute negligible independent explanatory power (delta AIC = 9.4 favoring the physical constraint model over the ecological adaptation model). The convergence of physical pointers from three independent domains provides a working framework for cardiac biophysics that generates specific, falsifiable predictions. All data are from publicly available published sources and can be independently verified.

title: Abstract 4369991: Small molecule inhibitors of serum glucocorticoid kinase 1 (SGK1) prevent cardiac structural and functional decline induced in a transverse aortic constriction (TAC) model
abstract: Introduction: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality despite current therapies. The transverse aortic constriction (TAC) model in rodent mimics conditions such as hypertension and aortic stenosis and is widely used to study HFrEF. SGK1, a stress activated kinase, plays a key role in cardiac remodeling, fibrosis, and inflammation, critical in HF progression. Genetic inhibition of SGK1 by cardiac-specific expression of dominant-negative SGK1 in a TAC model is shown to be cardioprotective. Small molecule inhibitors of SGK1 (SGK1i) have not previously been evaluated in the TAC model. Research Questions: To evaluate the efficacy of novel, potent and selective SGK1i in a TAC model. Methods: Male, Sprague Dawley Rats, that had undergone TAC (20G suture) or sham surgery were dosed once a day via oral gavage from Day 3 until the end of the study on Day 56 with vehicle, SGK1i A, or SGK1i B. All animals had echocardiography on Days 21, 28, 42 and 56 to monitor disease progression. Tissues were stained by picrosirius red, and collagen was quantified using ImageJ software. Results: SGK1i ameliorated the progression to heart failure following TAC compared to the vehicle treated group, noted by a higher ejection fraction in the SGK1i groups compared to the vehicle group that is apparent even at day 21 (EF%: Sham 71.93, Vehicle 59.27, SGK1i A 70.66, SGK1i B 72.20) and is sustained through day 56 (EF%: Sham 70.50, Vehicle 49.87, SGK1i A 65.28, SGK1i B 64.22). In addition, parameters of LV structure were preserved in the SGK1i groups through the course of the study (LVESV mL Day 56: Sham 0.11, Vehicle 0.23, SGK1i A 0.13, SGK1i B 0.13). Morphometric measurements confirmed a significant increase in HW/BW in vehicle treated animals, which was mitigated by SGK1i. Hemodynamic studies confirmed the beneficial effects of SGK1i compared to vehicle treated animals (LVEDP, stroke work preserved, LV elastance better), with SGK1i groups not significantly different from sham animals. Finally, histological analysis demonstrated significantly less fibrosis and myofibrillar disarray in similar sections of SGK1i treated versus vehicle groups. Conclusions: SGK1i prevented the development of TAC pressure overload-induced decline in systolic function, had beneficial effects on cardiac hypertrophy, and reduced fibrosis. These data support the continued development of SGK1 inhibitors as promising novel therapeutics for HF.

title: Coronary pericytes as mediators of brain–gut–heart signaling: expanding the cardioprotective paradigm of GLP-1
abstract: To the Editor, We read with great interest the study by Mastitskaya et al[1] describing a previously novel mechanism by which glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) exerts cardioprotective effects through the activation of ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channels in coronary pericytes. The authors elegantly demonstrate that GLP-1-mediated signaling promotes dilation of coronary capillaries by relaxing pericytes, thereby facilitating microvascular perfusion and limiting ischemia-related myocardial injury[1]. This work provides an important mechanistic framework linking gut-derived hormonal signaling, autonomic regulation, and coronary microvascular function. Coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD) remains a major determinant of adverse outcomes following myocardial ischemia and reperfusion. Even when epicardial coronary arteries are successfully reopened during primary percutaneous coronary intervention, the “no-reflow” phenomenon – characterized by impaired microvascular perfusion – affects a substantial proportion of patients and correlates with larger infarct size and increased mortality[2,3]. Although endothelial dysfunction and microvascular obstruction have traditionally been implicated, increasing evidence suggests that pericytes – contractile cells regulating capillary diameter – play a central role in controlling microvascular blood flow during ischemic injury[4,5]. The findings presented by Mastitskaya and colleagues place pericytes at the center of an integrative cardioprotective signaling axis. By demonstrating that GLP-1 activates KATP channels in coronary pericytes, the authors provide compelling evidence that these cells can directly respond to neurohumoral signals. Activation of these channels leads to hyperpolarization and relaxation of pericytes, allowing capillary dilation and improved perfusion of the ischemic myocardium[1,6]. This mechanism may help explain the microvascular benefits observed with GLP-1 signaling and highlights the therapeutic potential of targeting pericyte function in cardiovascular disease. A notable contribution of this study is the demonstration of a brain–gut–heart communication pathway mediated by vagal signaling. The concept that gastrointestinal hormones can influence cardiac microcirculation through neural circuits expands the traditional view of cardiometabolic regulation[7]. GLP-1 has long been recognized for its metabolic effects, and GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have demonstrated substantial cardiovascular benefits in clinical trials such as LEADER and SUSTAIN-6[8]. However, the precise mechanisms underlying these benefits are incompletely understood. The identification of a neurohumoral pathway linking GLP-1 signaling to coronary microvascular regulation offers a novel explanation for these clinical observations. Despite these advances, several critical questions remain. First, while Mastitskaya et al establish the functional necessity of pericyte KATP channels, the specific molecular subunits (e.g., Kir6.1 vs. Kir6.2) and the exact vagal brainstem nuclei – such as the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus – participating in this circuit require further anatomical and functional characterization[1,9]. Second, the translational gap between rodent models and human physiology is significant. While GLP-1RAs like semaglutide show promise, large-animal models (e.g., porcine) suggest that GLP-1 may also act through the RISK and SAFE molecular pathways or metabolic shifts via pyruvate dehydrogenase[10,11]. Furthermore, the interaction between GLP-1 signaling and other regulators of microvascular tone – such as nitric oxide and adenosine – warrants further investigation[12,13]. Understanding these interactions may reveal synergistic therapeutic strategies for preserving microvascular integrity. If GLP-1-mediated pericyte relaxation proves to be a generalizable mechanism, therapies targeting this pathway could have broad clinical applications in conditions characterized by CMD, including heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and diabetic cardiomyopathy[14,15]. In conclusion, the work by Mastitskaya et al highlights coronary pericytes as key mediators of GLP-1-induced cardioprotection and introduces a brain–gut–heart signaling axis regulating coronary microvascular perfusion. By emphasizing the role of pericytes in controlling microvascular blood flow and identifying neurohumoral pathways that influence their function, this study broadens the mechanistic understanding of GLP-1-mediated cardiovascular benefits and suggests new therapeutic opportunities targeting CMD.

title: Effects of blueberry extract and resistance training on the heart and lung structure and function in rats with experimental severe pulmonary arterial hypertension
abstract: The overall objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of blueberry extract and moderate-intensity resistance training (RT), either alone or in combination, on the heart and lung structure and function in a model of severe pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) induced by monocrotaline (MCT) in rats. In study 1, we evaluated the effects of blueberry extract and resistance training on lung and right ventricle (RV) function and structure in severe experimental PAH. Male Wistar rats were induced PAH by a single intraperitoneal injection of MCT (60 mg/kg). One day later, the animals started receiving blueberry extract (100 mg/kg daily by gavage) and were submitted to a three-week low-intensity resistance exercise protocol (ladder climbing - 15 climbs, 60s interval, 60% load, one session/day, 5 days/wk). After these treatments and echocardiographic assessment animals were euthanized and lung and RV samples were collected for mechanical, morphological, biochemical, and molecular analyses. Both blueberry extract and RT attenuated RV dysfunction (i.e., TAPSE) and pulmonary artery resistance (i.e., AT/ET) observed over the development of severe PAH. In addition, single RV myocyte mechanical function (i.e., shortening and velocities of shortening and relaxation) was maintained in treated rats. Moreover, the applied treatments mitigated oxidative imbalance [i.e., lung (SOD, CAT, GST, NO); RV (SOD, CAT, GST, NO and PC)] and structural remodeling [i.e., lung (i.e., alveolar septum, pulmonary alveoli, arteriole’s diameter, and total collagen); RV (total collagen and extracellular matrix)]. Furthermore, the interventions promoted partial or complete preservation of calcium regulatory proteins’ expression (i.e., RyR2, p-PLBSer16 and SERCA2a). In conclusion, blueberry extract and RT, either alone or in combination, alleviate cardiopulmonary oxidative imbalance and adverse structural remodeling, and sustain RV myocyte contractility and expression of calcium regulatory proteins and thus conserve pulmonary and RV function in severe PAH induced by monocrotaline. In study 2 we tested whether regular administration of blueberry extract and low-intensity RT, either alone or in combination, during the development of MCT induced severe PAH in rats, protect the left ventricle (LV) from redox dysregulation and pathological remodeling. Groups of seven male Wistar rats were formed for the experiment: sedentary control; sedentary hypertensive; sedentary hypertensive blueberry; exercise hypertensive; and exercise hypertensive blueberry. PAH was experimentally induced through a single intraperitoneal administration of MCT at a dose of 60 mg/kg. One day after injection, the blueberry groups started receiving a daily dose of blueberry extract (100 mg/kg) by gavage, while the exercise groups initiated a three-week program of RT (Ladder climbing; 15 climbs carrying 60% of maximum load; one session/day; 5 times/week). Echocardiographic evaluations were conducted 23 days after injection, and the rats were euthanized the next day to harvest LV tissue. Separately, blueberry extract and RT mitigated augments in pulmonary artery resistance, LV tissue’s redox dysregulation (i.e., increased PC levels) and detrimental remodeling (i.e., reduced inflammation), and reductions in ejection fraction (EF) and fractional shortening (FS) caused by PAH. The combination of treatments prevented reductions in EF and FS, as well as the development of a D-shaped LV. In conclusion, blueberry extract and moderate-intensity resistance training administered during the development of MCT- induced severe PAH in rats prevented LV redox dysregulation and pathological remodeling, thereby preserving its function. Together, these findings reinforce the potential of blueberry extract and resistance training, especially when combined, as promising non-pharmacological strategies in the management of severe PAH. title: FROM BENCH TO BEDSIDE: INVESTIGATING SGLT2 INHIBITORS AS A NOVEL STRATEGY AGAINST CHEMOTHERAPY-INDUCED CARDIOMYOPATHY
abstract: Therapeutic Area Pharmacologic Therapy Background Anthracyclines are essential components of chemotherapeutic regimens for a broad spectrum of malignancies, yet their utility is constrained by cumulative, dose-dependent cardiotoxicity, often culminating in non-ischemic cardiomyopathy and heart failure. The pathogenesis involves oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and topoisomerase IIβ–mediated DNA damage in cardiomyocytes. While ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) have demonstrated modest cardioprotective effects, the efficacy of newer heart failure therapies remains underexplored. Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, endorsed as Class I therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) per 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guidelines, have shown robust cardioprotective effects in large cardiovascular outcomes trials. However, their potential to prevent or attenuate anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity has not been systematically evaluated. This study aimed to assess preclinical and clinical evidence supporting their use in anthracycline-exposed populations. Methods A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Comprehensive searches of major medical databases and clinical trial registries were performed through March 2025. Eligible studies investigated SGLT2 inhibitors, beta-blockers, or ACE inhibitors in adult patients receiving anthracycline-based chemotherapy or in animal models replicating this exposure. Primary outcomes included changes in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), global longitudinal strain (GLS), and incidence of heart failure. Studies involving pre-existing heart failure or non-anthracyclinerelated cardiotoxicity were excluded. Results Preclinical studies (n=4) consistently demonstrated that SGLT2 inhibitors mitigated cardiomyocyte injury, fibrosis, and oxidative stress, preserving cardiac function in anthracycline-exposed models. In one study, LVEF was significantly higher in animals treated with SGLT2 inhibitors (61.3% ± 11%) versus controls (49.2% ± 8%, p = 0.007). Additional studies corroborated reduced histopathological damage and improved myocardial performance. No clinical trials to date have specifically assessed SGLT2 inhibitors in oncology populations. Nevertheless, major cardiovascular trials (e.g., EMPA-REG OUTCOME, DECLARE-TIMI 58) have demonstrated substantial reductions in heart failure events among non-cancer cohorts. In contrast, ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers have shown variable efficacy during chemotherapy, with inconsistent findings across studies. Conclusions SGLT2 inhibitors exhibit consistent cardioprotective effects in preclinical models of anthracycline cardiotoxicity and possess well-established efficacy in broader cardiovascular populations. These findings underscore the critical need for prospective trials evaluating their safety and therapeutic potential in cardio-oncology, with implications for reshaping current preventive strategies.

title: Topical vascular organoid therapy promotes microvascular regeneration and functional recovery in porcine ischemic cardiomyopathy
abstract: Ischemic heart disease (IHD) often progresses to heart failure due to persistent microvascular dysfunction not corrected by conventional epicardial revascularization. We developed a scaffold-free vascular organoid composed of human endothelial progenitor cells (EPCs) and mesenchymal stem cell-derived smooth muscle cells (SMCs) and evaluated its therapeutic potential in a porcine IHD model. Fourteen days after ischemia induction, bilayer EPC-SMC organoids were transplanted onto the left ventricular surface, and animals were followed for four weeks. Cardiac MRI demonstrated the preservation of left ventricular ejection fraction and modest improvement in regional function compared with controls. Histological and immunohistochemical analyses revealed the migration of transplanted cells into host myocardium, increased vascular density, and enhanced vessel maturation, while gene expression profiling showed the upregulation of angiogenesis-related genes. These findings demonstrate that scaffold-free EPC-SMC vascular organoids can engraft, promote microvascular remodeling, and preserve cardiac function after ischemic injury.

title: Exploring the MicroRNA Landscape in Cardiac Amyloidosis: Molecular Insights and Clinical Applications
abstract: Background: Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is an increasingly recognized cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, resulting from myocardial deposition of misfolded amyloid fibrils derived predominantly from transthyretin (ATTR wild-type [ATTRwt] or variant [ATTRv]) or immunoglobulin light chains (AL). Despite advances in noninvasive imaging and disease-modifying therapies, delayed diagnosis remains common, and clinically actionable molecular biomarkers for early detection, phenotypic discrimination, and therapeutic monitoring are limited. MicroRNAs (miRNAs), small noncoding regulators of post-transcriptional gene expression, have emerged as key modulators of cardiovascular remodeling and systemic amyloid biology. Methods: We performed a comprehensive review of experimental, translational, and clinical studies to evaluate the role of miRNAs in transthyretin and light-chain cardiac amyloidosis, incorporating data from myocardial tissue analyses, circulating miRNA profiling, and mechanistic studies in cellular and animal models. Results: Dysregulated miRNA networks contribute to amyloid-induced cardiac injury by modulating mitochondrial energetics, oxidative stress, inflammation, fibrosis, proteostasis, and neurocardiac signaling. Specific miRNAs, including members of the miR-21, miR-29, and miR-30 families, as well as miR-150-5p and miR-339, have been associated with amyloid burden, adverse myocardial remodeling, plasma cell biology, and disease severity. Distinct circulating and tissue miRNA signatures differentiate transthyretin from light-chain cardiac amyloidosis and correlate with functional status, heart failure biomarkers, and clinical outcomes. Conclusions: MiRNAs represent promising diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers in cardiac amyloidosis and offer mechanistic insights into disease pathogenesis. Integration of miRNA profiling with multimodality imaging and emerging RNA-based therapeutics may enable earlier diagnosis and support precision management of amyloid-related heart failure.

title: Tirzepatide attenuates doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity via mitochondrial function improvement
abstract: BACKGROUND: Doxorubicin (DOX) is a highly effective anthracycline chemotherapeutic agent, but its clinical utility is severely limited by dose-dependent cardiotoxicity, which can lead to irreversible heart failure. This study investigated the cardioprotective potential of tirzepatide, a novel dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist, against DOX-induced cardiac injury. METHODS: We established comprehensive in vitro and in vivo injury models. Cardiac systolic function was quantitatively assessed via transthoracic echocardiography, measuring left ventricular ejection fraction and fractional shortening. Histopathological evaluation of myocardial structure was performed using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. Mitochondrial ultrastructure integrity, particularly cristae morphology, was examined via transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) was measured using the fluorescent JC-1 probe. RESULTS: Tirzepatide treatment significantly attenuated DOX-induced cardiotoxicity. It markedly improved left ventricular systolic function and reduced histopathological damage. Crucially, tirzepatide preserved mitochondrial integrity, evidenced by TEM showing maintained cristae density and structure, and effectively restored DOX-induced MMP dissipation, indicating rescued mitochondrial bioenergetic function. CONCLUSIONS: Tirzepatide confers significant cardioprotection against DOX-induced toxicity in both cellular and animal models. The primary mechanism underlying this protection is the amelioration of DOX-triggered mitochondrial dysfunction, specifically through the preservation of cristae integrity and restoration of MMP. These findings strongly support further investigation of tirzepatide as a promising adjunctive therapy to enhance the cardiac safety profile of DOX chemotherapy.
